common_name: Dawson's White Brunnera (Wide Cream-Margined Siberian Bugloss)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in evenly moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; the cream margins expand through the season and can be unstable, so remove any all-green reverted shoots as soon as they appear.

directions: Grow in consistently moist, organically rich soil in dappled to full shade, since the bold ivory-white leaf margins scorch quickly in direct sun or dry spells. Named for the Dutch gardener who brought it into cultivation decades before the more uniform Jack Frost line was introduced, Dawson's White carries heart-shaped green leaves edged in irregular, hand-painted-looking cream that widens as the season progresses. Because the variegation pattern can revert to solid green on individual shoots, walk the clump periodically and cut those stems back to the crown to keep the planting looking crisp. It combines well with ferns and dark-leaved heucheras where its pale edges catch available light.

common_name: Mr. Morse Brunnera (White-Flowered Frosted Silver Bugloss)

planting.note: Plant container divisions in early spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; established clumps tolerate brief dry spells better than most brunnera cultivars.

directions: Site in humus-rich, evenly moist soil in partial shade, allowing a bit more morning sun than Jack Frost tolerates. Bred in Belgium from a cross of 'Betty Bowring' and 'Inspector Morse', this cultivar carries heavily silvered, green-veined leaves in the classic frosted brunnera style but blooms in clean white rather than the usual sky blue, giving it a cooler, more understated look in a shaded bed. Its improved tolerance of drier soil makes it a dependable choice under high tree canopies where irrigation is inconsistent. Divide congested clumps in early spring or after flowering to maintain vigor.

common_name: Jack's Gold Brunnera (Gold-Edged Silver Heartleaf Bugloss)

planting.note: Plant divisions in cool, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; provide a little more shade than a straight-silver brunnera to prevent the gold edge from scorching.

directions: Grow in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in a cool, sheltered spot with dappled to full shade. Arising as a sport of Jack Frost, this cultivar opens each spring with foliage flushed soft gold before settling into the familiar silver overlay on heart-shaped leaves, this time trimmed with a persistent narrow band of yellow-green at the margin. Airy sprays of small blue forget-me-not flowers rise above the foliage in mid-spring. Slugs generally avoid the leaves, so it pairs safely with hostas in a mixed shade border without needing extra pest management.

common_name: Twinkle Toes Lungwort (Compact Silver-Spotted Pulmonaria)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in early spring or fall in humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil in shade to part sun; performs reliably in dry shade once established.

directions: Plant in humus-rich soil that retains moisture without staying soggy, in shade to part sun. Twinkle Toes was named a Perennial Plant of the Year for its unusually compact, tidy habit and strong mildew resistance, traits that set it apart from older, floppier lungwort selections. Deep green leaves flecked with silver spots support a long three-week run of periwinkle-blue flowers in mid-spring, and the plant continues to look presentable through summer without the leaf collapse common to less resistant cultivars. It is a good choice for smaller shaded borders or containers where a well-mannered groundcover is needed.

common_name: Victorian Brooch Pulmonaria (Long-Blooming Magenta-Coral Lungwort)

planting.note: Plant divisions in organically rich, evenly moist soil in part to full shade; cut foliage back hard after the extended bloom period to refresh the silver-spotted leaves for summer.

directions: Site in rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in part or full shade. A Terra Nova hybrid bred for flower power, Victorian Brooch produces clusters of vivid magenta-coral blooms held just above long, densely silver-spotted foliage, and remains in bloom for up to ten weeks — noticeably longer than most lungwort cultivars. Its low, spreading habit and good resistance to powdery mildew make it useful as an edging plant along shaded paths or at the front of a woodland bed. Shearing the plant back after flowering encourages fresh new foliage that stays attractive into fall.

common_name: E.B. Anderson Lungwort (Narrow-Leaf Silver-Spotted Longleaf Pulmonaria)

planting.note: Plant divisions in ordinary, moisture-retentive garden soil in part shade to full shade; avoid deep dry shade where the narrow leaves are less forgiving of drought than broader-leaved lungworts.

directions: Grow in humus-rich soil that does not dry out for long stretches, positioned in part to full shade. Honoring the noted British plantsman for whom it is named, this narrow-leaved longleaf lungwort forms a low tuft of slender, dark green leaves heavily spotted in silver, with clusters of small flowers that open pink and mature to deep blue in early spring. Its neat, compact habit makes it useful at the front of a shaded border or tucked among ferns and hellebores where a broader lungwort would crowd its neighbors. It is one of the earliest lungworts to flower, providing nectar before most other shade perennials are active.

common_name: Pink Elf Epimedium (Dwarf Magenta-Spurred Barrenwort)

planting.note: Plant divisions in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; the slow-spreading wiry rootstock tolerates dry shade under trees once established.

directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, where it slowly spreads into a dwarf, wiry-stemmed clump. A hybrid of Epimedium leptorrhizum and E. pubigerum, Pink Elf carries new foliage flushed bronze in spring, followed by nodding sprays of pale pink outer sepals surrounding a deeper pink-purple cup in early spring. Its compact scale suits small woodland gardens or rock-garden edges where larger epimediums would overwhelm the space. Cut back old evergreen foliage in late winter just before new growth emerges to display the flowers clearly.

common_name: Enchantress Epimedium (Soft Pink Arching-Spray Barrenwort)

planting.note: Plant divisions in humus-rich, well-drained soil in bright shade to full shade; drought tolerant once established but benefits from regular moisture the first season.

directions: Grow in humus-rich, well-drained soil in bright to full shade beneath deciduous trees or shrubs. Bred by plantswoman Elizabeth Strangman from a cross of Epimedium dolichostemon and E. leptorrhizum, Enchantress produces neat, small flowers in a gentle silvery pink, arranged in elegant arching sprays above narrow evergreen leaflets, a daintier and more refined effect than many larger-flowered epimediums. Once established the wiry rhizomes tolerate the dry soil common under mature trees, making it a reliable long-term groundcover for difficult shaded sites. Trim old foliage back in late winter to showcase the spring flower display.

common_name: William Stearn Epimedium (Dark Red Yellow-Tipped Barrenwort)

planting.note: Plant divisions in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; evergreen foliage benefits from a light trim of tattered leaves in late winter.

directions: Site in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath trees or tall shrubs. Named for the eminent Epimedium botanist, this clump-forming, rhizomatous selection carries evergreen, heart-shaped leaflets that emerge mottled with dark red splashes before maturing to green, providing season-long foliage interest even before the flowers appear. In spring it produces very dark red flowers with pale pink, yellow-tipped spurs, a richer and moodier color combination than most barrenworts offer. Because the foliage persists through winter in milder zones, groom out tattered old leaves before new growth begins so the flowers are not obscured.

common_name: Black Snowflake Tiarella (Deeply Cut Dark-Veined Foamflower)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial sun to full shade; forms a non-invasive, slowly expanding clump.

directions: Grow in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial sun to full shade, mulching lightly to keep roots cool. Black Snowflake is prized for its dramatically dissected, almost lacy foliage traced with wide, near-black veins radiating out from the leaf center, a pattern that intensifies during cool spring and fall weather. In mid-spring the plant sends up numerous slender spikes of lightly fragrant, star-shaped white flowers well above the foliage. Its clump-forming, non-spreading habit makes it a tidy choice for edging a shaded bed or tucking among spring bulbs whose fading foliage it will help disguise.

common_name: Timbuktu Tiarella (Crimson-Veined Cut-Leaf Foamflower)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; spreads slowly by runners into a dense mat over several seasons.

directions: Plant in fertile, consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Timbuktu carries deeply cut, semi-evergreen foliage traced with bold crimson to purple coloration along and near the veins, giving the clump rich color even before bloom. In spring it produces abundant spikes of white flowers lightly blushed pink that draw bees and other pollinators. Unlike strictly clumping foamflowers, Timbuktu spreads gradually by runners to form a low, weed-suppressing mat, making it a useful groundcover choice for a shaded woodland path or under high-branching shrubs.

common_name: Pink Bouquet Tiarella (Low Pink-Flowered Foamflower)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in cool, moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; tolerates drier soil once established but colors best with consistent moisture.

directions: Site in cool, moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade. Pink Bouquet forms a compact, semi-evergreen mound of deeply lobed leaves marked with wine-toned veins, with new growth showing a chocolate-brown cast that mellows to lime green through the season and warms to bronze-red again in fall. Its flower spikes stay noticeably shorter than those of most tiarellas, so the pale pink, star-shaped blooms open in dense, low bouquets right at the top of the foliage mound rather than on tall separate stems. This low profile and readiness to spread by runners make it a strong choice for the front edge of a shaded border or as a container specimen.

common_name: Ivory Hearts Bleeding Heart (Compact White Reblooming Dicentra)

planting.note: Divide and replant clumps in early spring while dormant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; blooms longest where summers stay relatively cool.

directions: Grow in humus-rich, evenly moist but well-drained soil in partial to full shade, tucking plants where their compact form and extended bloom can be enjoyed up close. A hybrid between the Asian Dicentra peregrina and the native fringed bleeding heart D. eximia, Ivory Hearts forms a tidy dome of finely cut, blue-green, fern-like foliage topped by arching stems of clean ivory-white, heart-shaped flowers held well above the leaves. It reblooms over an unusually long season, particularly in regions with cool summers, and its strong rhizomatous roots make it a durable, long-lived edging plant for a shaded rock garden or woodland border.

common_name: Bacchanal Bleeding Heart (Deep Crimson Pacific Dicentra)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in rich, evenly moist soil in partial to full shade; spreads gently by rhizomes to form a colony over a few seasons.

directions: Plant in rich, consistently moist soil in partial to full shade, where the spreading rhizomes will slowly knit together into an attractive colony. Bacchanal, an Award of Garden Merit selection of the Pacific bleeding heart, produces finely divided, gray-green, fern-like foliage topped by short clusters of nodding, deep crimson to red-violet flowers in late spring. Established plantings often pause flowering in summer heat and resume a second flush as temperatures cool in late summer or fall, especially where afternoon shade is reliable. It is deer and rabbit resistant and combines well with ferns and hostas in a naturalistic shade planting.

common_name: Fubuki Japanese Forest Grass (Compact White-Striped Hakonechloa)

planting.note: Plant container divisions in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in part to full shade; compact habit suits containers as well as border edges.

directions: Grow in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in part to full shade. Discovered as a sport within a batch of 'Aureola' seedlings, Fubuki (Japanese for "snowstorm") carries green blades finely striped with white rather than gold, on a noticeably shorter, more compact mound than most Hakonechloa selections. Its tidy, dense habit makes it well suited to containers, small border edges, or mass plantings where a lower-growing texture is wanted. Blades take on a soft pinkish flush as cooler fall temperatures arrive, extending the season of interest beyond the summer display.

common_name: Stripe It Rich Japanese Forest Grass (Compact Gold-and-White Hakonechloa)

planting.note: Plant container divisions in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in part to full shade; its dense, compact clump is well suited to small spaces and containers.

directions: Site in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in part to full shade to keep the fine variegation from scorching. Originating as a tissue-culture mutation of the unpatented golden cultivar 'All Gold', Stripe It Rich carries golden blades further striped with crisp white, arranged in a dense, spreading clump noticeably shorter than most Hakonechloa selections. Its compact size and bright color make it a strong choice for edging a shaded path, filling a small container, or brightening the front of a mixed shade border. Like other Hakonechloa cultivars it resents heavy or poorly drained soil, so amend clay soils generously with organic matter before planting.

common_name: Pink Elf Ajuga (Coppery-Purple Pink-Flowered Bugleweed)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in partial shade to shade; spreads by surface stolons and fills in quickly for groundcover use.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in partial shade to full shade, where the low mat will spread by surface stolons to knit together within a season or two. Pink Elf forms a dense carpet of glossy, coppery-purple foliage noticeably lower-growing than many ajuga cultivars, punctuated in spring by short, dense spikes of soft pinkish-mauve flowers that stand just above the leaf mat. Its compact scale and tolerance of both moist shade and, with adequate watering, brighter sites make it a versatile edging or small-space groundcover for shaded borders, rock walls, or areas with light foot traffic. Divide congested patches every few years to renew vigor and prevent crown crowding.

common_name: Braunherz Ajuga (Nearly Black Bronze-Red Bugleweed)

planting.note: Plant divisions in well-drained, average soil in partial to full shade with good air circulation; avoid heavy, poorly drained sites to reduce risk of crown rot.

directions: Grow in well-drained, average soil in partial to full shade, providing good air movement to reduce the risk of crown rot in humid climates. Also sold as 'Bronze Heart', Braunherz forms a very low, dense carpet of rounded, reddish-bronze leaves that darken to nearly black as they mature, among the darkest foliage available in the genus. Short spikes of deep blue flowers appear in mid-spring, standing out sharply against the dark leaf color. The mat is essentially semi-evergreen in mild winters but can look ragged after a harsh one, so groom out damaged foliage in early spring before new growth resumes.

common_name: Anne Greenaway Lamium (Chartreuse-and-Silver Variegated Dead Nettle)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in bright shade to shade; shear back in midsummer if foliage fades from heat.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in bright shade to full shade. Anne Greenaway produces scallop-edged leaves that open lemon-yellow in spring before settling into a multi-toned mix of chartreuse, silver, and mint green through the growing season, giving it more color variation than most lamium cultivars. Spikes of lilac-purple flowers appear intermittently from mid-spring into early fall, drawing bees over an unusually long bloom window. Its trailing habit spreads quickly into a dense mat, making it equally useful as a groundcover under trees, a trailing accent in mixed containers, or a filler along a shaded rock wall.

common_name: Shell Pink Lamium (Pale Pink White-Centered Dead Nettle)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; tolerates dry shade and a range of soil types once established.

directions: Site in moist to average, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, where this stoloniferous groundcover will spread readily to fill gaps. Shell Pink bears green, heart-shaped, scalloped leaves marked with a bright white diamond down the center, topped by loose clusters of soft, pale pink hooded flowers beginning in mid-spring with intermittent rebloom into fall. It adapts to a wide range of soils, including heavy clay, and tolerates drier shade better than many groundcovers once its roots are established. Use it beneath shrubs or shade trees where turf struggles, or let it trail from a shaded container or hanging basket.
